"Taking Job For Error In Judgment Seems Quite Harsh Punishment," Says Head Of Police Union – Follow-up

http://www.pioneerplanet.com/info/pioneerpress.htm

February 27, 1998,

By Robert F. Moore Staff Writer

A highly decorated St. Paul police officer was terminated Tuesday after testing positive for marijuana use, according to sources in the department.
Sgt. Cregg Brackman, 47, the lead investigator in the St. Paul case against suspected serial rapist Tony Dejuan Jackson, confirmed his dismissal Thursday afternoon.

Brackman, a 21-year department veteran, was honored by his peers as state sex crimes investigator of the year for his role in connecting the four rapes Jackson is accused of committing last year. Jackson is currently on trial in Washington County on the first of four rape charges.

Brackman also has worked with investigators in Mason City, Iowa, on the 1995 disappearance of television anchorwoman Jodi Huisentruit.

Brackman declined to comment on the specific charges against him but said he plans to appeal.

St. Paul Police Chief William Finney would not discuss the action against Brackman on Thursday afternoon, saying he could not comment on pending disciplinary actions until their final disposition.

He did, however, speak generally about the seriousness with which the department views illegal drug use by police officers.

"We have a zero-tolerance policy in the St. Paul Police Department," said Finney. "If someone were found to have illegal drugs in their system, we would dismiss them immediately."

Brackman allegedly was implicated by a woman arrested in Dakota County who offered the sergeant’s name in an effort to lessen her culpability, sources said. An investigation into the woman’s claim by the East Metro Drug Task Force resulted in a failed urinalysis test, sources said.

It could not be confirmed whether it was Brackman’s first drug infraction, though Finney said no St. Paul officer had ever been terminated for drug use before. The zero-tolerance policy, he said, is a federal mandate adopted before his tenure began in 1992.

St. Paul police officers can be ordered by the chief to submit to drug tests only if they work on the Critical Incident Response Team or the bomb squad. Officers in other units can be ordered to submit to a urinalysis "under the concurrence of two supervisors" who, based on an officer’s behavior or reliable information, reasonably suspect the officer of using an illegal substance, Finney said.

Several officers within the department called the firing of Brackman, who is white, an example of preferential treatment given African-Americans under the administration of Finney, who is black. They cited the case of a black parking enforcement officer who failed a drug test more than two years ago while serving in that non-sworn position. That person then entered a department drug rehabilitation program and passed a urinalysis test. He then became a sworn officer about 18 months ago.

Finney defended that action on grounds that sworn police officers are held to a higher standard and that the person in question was not a sworn officer at the time of the failed test.

Meanwhile, St. Paul attorney Mark Gehan, who often represents officers who are in the Police Federation, said Brackman has 21 days to file a grievance over his dismissal, if he chooses to appeal through that route. Gehan has yet to be assigned to the case.

The Saint Paul Pioneer Press is Minnesota’s oldest newspaper, beginning as the Minnesota Pioneer in 1849.
